title: 5  Cloud execution mental model: AWS and transferable concepts
text:
5.18 Practical 2: miniature paid AWS lab
This optional practical creates real cloud resources and can incur charges. It uses synthetic data and has two stages:

store and verify one tiny object in S3; and
run the official AWS Batch Fargate hello-world job.

AWS estimates its Fargate CLI tutorial at less than USD $0.01 if resources are removed promptly, but that is not a guarantee of your total bill. Prices, taxes, existing account resources, public IPv4 charges and Regions differ. Check current pricing before starting. Set a personal ceiling such as $5 that you are genuinely willing to pay.






WarningBudget alerts are delayed, not hard caps



AWS states that budget information can be delayed and is updated only several times per day. A $5 alert does not automatically prevent $6 of spending. The controls in this lab are tiny inputs, no NAT gateway, short execution, immediate teardown and verification.



5.18.1 Phase 0 — authorization and guardrails
Use a personal learning account only if you are authorized to create charges. Do not use an employer account without approval. Secure the root user with MFA, do not create root access keys and use a non-root federated or IAM identity for normal work.
In Billing and Cost Management → Budgets, create a monthly cost budget. A reasonable learning configuration is:

budget amount: $5 USD;
actual-cost alerts: $1, $3 and $5;
alert destination: an email address you actively monitor; and
no assumption that the alert terminates resources.

Follow AWS’s current cost-budget procedure. Also inspect the account’s current Cost Explorer/billing view so pre-existing costs are not attributed to this lab.
Write down:
spending ceiling accepted: yes/no
budget configured: yes/no
account contains other resources: yes/no/unknown
chosen Region:
start time:
Stop if the first two answers are not yes.


5.18.2 Phase 1 — open CloudShell and prove identity
Open AWS CloudShell in the chosen Region. AWS provides CloudShell without an additional CloudShell charge, although resources created from it are billable. Its browser session supplies temporary credentials, so this exercise does not need a local access key.
Set one Region and inspect the caller:
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="$AWS_REGION"

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure get region
Replace us-east-1 if you intentionally selected another Region. Confirm that the account and ARN are the learning identity you expected. Do not paste the complete account ID into a public repository.
Create collision-resistant lab names from the current account:
LAB_ACCOUNT_ID="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)"
LAB_SUFFIX="$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)"
LAB_BUCKET="nf-biologist-${LAB_ACCOUNT_ID}-${LAB_SUFFIX}"

printf 'region=%s\nbucket=%s\n' "$AWS_REGION" "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  > cloud-lab-state.txt
cloud-lab-state.txt is your cleanup record. It contains an account-derived bucket name, so keep it local rather than committing it.


5.18.3 Phase 2 — create, verify and remove a tiny S3 object
Create a four-line synthetic FASTQ-like fixture:
printf '@synthetic-read-1\nACGTACGT\n+\nFFFFFFFF\n' > mini.fastq
sha256sum mini.fastq
Create the bucket. us-east-1 has special bucket-creation syntax:
if [ "$AWS_REGION" = "us-east-1" ]; then
  aws s3api create-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION"
else
  aws s3api create-bucket \
    --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
    --region "$AWS_REGION" \
    --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION"
fi
Block public access explicitly:
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  'BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true'
Upload, list and download the object:
aws s3 cp mini.fastq "s3://${LAB_BUCKET}/inputs/mini.fastq"
aws s3 ls "s3://${LAB_BUCKET}/inputs/"
aws s3 cp "s3://${LAB_BUCKET}/inputs/mini.fastq" mini.downloaded.fastq
Compare the bytes:
sha256sum mini.fastq mini.downloaded.fastq
cmp mini.fastq mini.downloaded.fastq
echo "cmp_exit_code=$?"
An exit code of 0 and matching hashes prove byte identity. They do not prove that a real FASTQ has valid pairing, read counts or biological provenance.
Inspect the controls rather than assuming them:
aws s3api get-bucket-location --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
aws s3api head-object --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --key inputs/mini.fastq
Now remove only the known object, verify the bucket is empty, then remove it:
aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --key inputs/mini.fastq

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --query 'Contents[].Key'

aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION"
The list should return no keys before delete-bucket. Verify deletion:
aws s3api head-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
echo "expected_nonzero_after_deletion=$?"
The final call should fail because the bucket no longer exists or is no longer accessible. This is an intentional negative test.


5.18.4 Phase 3 — run one tiny AWS Batch Fargate job
Use AWS’s maintained AWS Batch Fargate CLI tutorial, not a copied third-party command sequence. It takes approximately 15–20 minutes and walks through:

creating the Batch task execution role;
creating a Fargate compute environment;
creating a job queue;
registering a small job definition;
submitting and monitoring one job;
reading its CloudWatch log; and
disabling and deleting the queue and compute environment and removing the remaining tutorial resources.

Before executing each tutorial command, replace its names with a clear prefix such as nf-biologist-lab- and check that AWS_REGION is still correct:
aws sts get-caller-identity
printf 'Region: %s\n' "$AWS_REGION"
Do not add a NAT gateway, large data, GPUs or a long-running service. Choose Fargate and use the tutorial’s stated CPU, memory and single short hello-world command. Fargate accepts only specific CPU/memory combinations; do not enlarge the request merely because more capacity sounds safer.
Capture this evidence in cloud-batch-evidence.txt:
Region:
job name:
job ID:
final Batch status:
container image/tag or digest:
requested vCPU and memory:
CloudWatch log group/stream:
first and last log timestamps:
job output summary:
cleanup completion time:
Do not publish raw account IDs, ARNs or logs until you have reviewed them.


5.18.5 Phase 4 — prove cleanup
Follow the tutorial cleanup in dependency order. Batch generally requires a queue or compute environment to be disabled before it can be deleted. Wait for the reported state instead of repeatedly issuing deletion commands.
Then inspect, rather than assume:
aws batch describe-job-queues
aws batch describe-compute-environments
aws batch describe-job-definitions --status ACTIVE
aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[].Name'
Filter the output for your nf-biologist-lab- prefix. Confirm that no lab queue, compute environment, active job definition or bucket remains. Review the IAM role and CloudWatch log group created by the tutorial and remove them if the tutorial’s cleanup did not do so. Do not delete unrelated resources.
Record:
lab bucket absent: yes/no
lab queue absent: yes/no
lab compute environment absent: yes/no
lab job definition inactive/removed: yes/no
lab IAM role removed: yes/no
lab log group retained or removed intentionally:
end time:
Check the billing dashboard later because cost data is delayed. The goal is not to claim a universal exact price; it is to connect each observed charge to a resource and prove that no billable lab resource was left running.


5.18.6 Optional extension — understand ECR without retaining an image
If you already understand Docker and want to practice the registry layer, follow the official ECR getting-started procedure with a tiny image. Record both tag and digest, pull by digest, then delete the image and repository immediately. Review current ECR storage and transfer pricing first. This extension is intentionally optional because Chapter 9 teaches image construction in depth.

text:
5.21 Ten interview questions

5.21.1 1. What is the difference between AWS Batch and Fargate?


Model answer

AWS Batch is the scheduling/orchestration layer: it accepts jobs, evaluates queues and places work. Fargate is one compute option that supplies serverless container capacity. Batch can also use managed EC2 capacity. A complete answer names both layers because they affect cost, capability and operations differently.



5.21.2 2. Why is an S3 prefix not a normal directory?


Model answer

S3 stores objects identified by bucket and key. Slash-separated prefixes give keys a hierarchical appearance, but there is no POSIX directory tree with the same rename, locking, permissions and random-access semantics. Applications must use an object API or an integration that deliberately translates those semantics.



5.21.3 3. A Batch job says SUCCEEDED. Is the analysis valid?


Model answer

No. It means the scheduled command reported successful completion. I would also verify input identity and checksums, workflow revision, image digest, parameters, expected outputs and domain metrics such as read counts, FastQC, mapping statistics and sample identity.



5.21.4 4. Why should a workload use an IAM role instead of an access key in its image?


Model answer

A role provides temporary, rotatable credentials to the workload and can be scoped with least-privilege policies. A key baked into an image is long-lived, can be copied with every image pull, is difficult to rotate and turns the image registry into a credential exposure path.



5.21.5 5. Why does a budget alert not guarantee a spending cap?


Model answer

Billing data and budget evaluation are delayed, and an alert is ordinarily a notification rather than an immediate resource kill switch. Cost control also requires quotas and policy where appropriate, small initial tests, bounded resources, ownership, monitoring and explicit teardown.



5.21.6 6. Why pin a container digest if the image already has a version tag?


Model answer

A registry tag is a reference that can be moved to different content. A digest is content-addressed and identifies the exact image manifest. I can retain a readable version tag for discovery while recording or executing the digest for reproducibility.



5.21.7 7. What belongs in the Nextflow S3 work directory, and why does lifecycle matter?


Model answer

The work directory contains staged task inputs, commands, metadata and outputs used for execution and resume. It can grow much larger than final results. Deleting it too early breaks resume and audit needs; retaining it indefinitely creates cost and governance problems. Retention must reflect recovery, reproducibility, policy and whether the data can be recomputed.



5.21.8 8. How would you investigate AccessDenied safely?


Model answer

I would identify the caller, denied API action, exact resource and relevant identity/resource/key policies. I would decide whether the action is actually required, then grant the narrowest justified permission and retest. I would not attach administrator access merely to make the error disappear.



5.21.9 9. Why can data transfer dominate an apparently cheap compute design?


Model answer

Genomics inputs and intermediates are large. Repeated downloads, cross-Region movement, internet egress or traffic through charged networking components can outweigh a short compute task. I place compute near approved data, minimize unnecessary copies and model storage requests and transfer explicitly.



5.21.10 10. What must you verify before moving human genomic data to a cloud account?


Model answer

I need institutional approval and evidence for consented use, data classification, contracts, permitted account and Region, identity and least privilege, encryption/key governance, networking, logging, retention, backup, deletion and incident response. Technical encryption alone does not establish legal or organizational authorization.

text:
6.1 Why a biologist should care
A computational result depends on more than FASTQ files and a tool name. It also depends on scripts, workflow definitions, parameters, environment files, container recipes and decisions that change over time.
Without version control, files often evolve like this:
Those names do not answer:
Git records deliberate snapshots and the relationships between them. It gives software changes a reviewable history. It does not decide whether the biology is correct; it makes the exact analytical instructions available for review.
AI increases the need for this discipline. If an assistant edits eight files, you need a way to inspect the exact patch, separate useful changes from unrelated ones and preserve the accepted state.

text:
6.3 Repository, working tree and .git
A repository is a project whose history Git manages. In a normal local repository you see the project files plus a hidden .git directory:
git-first-repo/
├── .git/            Git's database and local configuration
├── .gitignore       tracked rules for intentionally untracked paths
├── README.md        project explanation
└── workflow.md      example analytical plan
The working tree is the checked-out collection of ordinary files you edit. The .git directory stores commits, references, configuration and other metadata. Deleting .git does not delete the visible project files, but it removes that local repository’s Git history and identity.






WarningDo not edit .git by hand



Use Git commands to inspect and change repository state. Directly modifying files inside .git can corrupt or misdirect the repository.

section: 6.4 The staging area is a proposed next snapshot
text:
6.4 The staging area is a proposed next snapshot
The staging area—also called the index—is the content currently selected for the next commit.
Imagine that you edit README.md and workflow.md, but only the README is ready. You can stage only that file:
git add README.md
Now the repository contains three relevant versions:

the last committed README.md;
the staged README proposed for the next commit; and
any additional unstaged edits in the working tree.

This is why “I saved the file” and “I committed the change” are different.

6.5 The five file states








State
Meaning
Useful evidence




Untracked
File exists but has never been selected for Git
git status


Tracked and unchanged
Working copy matches the selected commit
clean git status


Modified
Tracked file differs from the index/commit
git diff


Staged
Content is selected for the next commit
git diff --staged


Committed
Snapshot is stored in local history
git log, git show

section: 6.6 Commits are snapshots connected by history
text:
6.6 Commits are snapshots connected by history
A commit records:

a snapshot of tracked content;
a reference to its parent commit or commits;
author and committer information;
timestamps; and
a message.

Git identifies a commit using a cryptographic object ID. You often see an abbreviated form such as:
a17c42e docs: describe the synthetic test fixture
Changing commit content or metadata produces a different ID. A commit ID is therefore more precise than “the latest version,” but an abbreviated ID should be long enough to remain unique in the repository.
Git is conceptually snapshot-based, even though commands such as git diff show changes between snapshots.

text:
6.7 Branches and HEAD
A branch is a movable name pointing to a commit. main is a common default branch name. When you create a new commit on main, the branch advances to the new commit.
HEAD normally identifies the branch currently checked out:
HEAD ──► main ──► newest commit ──► parent commit
This model explains why a branch is cheap: it is primarily a reference, not a second full copy of every project file.
Branches, switching and merging are developed in Chapter 7. For now, remain on one local branch and learn to inspect it.

text:
6.8 Git identity is not authentication
Every commit stores an author name and email. Configure them for this practice repository:
git config --local user.name "Your Name"
git config --local user.email "you@example.org"
--local writes configuration for the current repository. It avoids silently changing every repository on a shared or institutional machine.
Inspect the result:
git config --local --get user.name
git config --local --get user.email
This identity is attribution, not proof that you can access GitHub. SSH keys, HTTPS tokens and federated login are authentication mechanisms discussed in Chapter 8.

text:
6.10 .gitignore controls untracked discovery
A .gitignore file contains patterns for paths Git should normally leave untracked. A small workflow project might begin with:
# Workflow runtime state
work/
.nextflow/
.nextflow.log*

# Generated data and results
data/
results/
*.bam
*.bai
*.fastq
*.fastq.gz

# Local environments and container artifacts
.conda/
conda-envs/
containers/
*.sif

# Secrets
.env
*.pem
*.key

# Operating-system/editor files
.DS_Store
*~
Patterns are project decisions. If data/ contains a deliberately tiny public fixture that should be tracked, ignoring the entire directory would be too broad. You might instead ignore data/raw/ and explicitly retain data/test/mini.fastq.
Important limitation: .gitignore does not make an already tracked file untracked, remove it from old commits or protect a secret. If a secret entered history, stop using it, revoke/rotate it and follow your organization’s incident procedure.
Test an ignore decision:
git check-ignore -v path/to/file
This prints the matching rule and its source. No output usually means that path is not ignored.

text:
6.11 The inspection commands form a safety loop

6.11.1 git status: classify current state
git status
git status --short
The long form teaches what is staged and unstaged. The short form is compact once you understand the two status columns.
Examples:
?? notes.md       untracked
 M README.md      modified in working tree
M  workflow.md    staged change
MM config.yml     staged content plus additional unstaged edits


6.11.2 git diff: inspect unstaged changes
git diff
git diff -- README.md
This compares the working tree with the staging area. It does not show newly untracked file contents.


6.11.3 git diff --staged: inspect the proposed commit
git diff --staged
This is the final review before git commit. If the output contains a key, patient identifier, large generated file or unrelated edit, do not commit it.
--cached is a synonym:
git diff --cached


6.11.4 git ls-files: list what Git tracks
git ls-files
This is more reliable than looking at the directory. A file can exist locally without being part of the repository.


6.11.5 git log and git show: inspect recorded history
git log --oneline --decorate
git show --stat HEAD
git show HEAD
git log shows commit history. git show displays one commit’s metadata and patch. HEAD means the currently selected commit.

text:
6.12 Practical: create your first local repository
This exercise creates a disposable repository with no cloud account, remote or biological data. Run it somewhere outside another Git repository.

6.12.1 Step 0 — verify the location
pwd
git --version
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
For the third command, a failure is desirable if you intend to create a new standalone repository. If it prints an existing parent repository, move to a different location before continuing.






WarningNested repositories confuse beginners



Running git init inside an existing repository creates a nested repository. That can be intentional, but it is not this exercise. Always inspect git rev-parse --show-toplevel first.




6.12.2 Step 1 — create and initialize the project
mkdir git-first-repo
cd git-first-repo

git init -b main
git status
If an older Git version does not support -b, use:
git init
git branch -M main
Confirm the repository root and branch:
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
git branch --show-current
Expected branch: main.


6.12.3 Step 2 — configure repository-local attribution
git config --local user.name "Your Name"
git config --local user.email "you@example.org"

git config --local --list
Use your real professional attribution if this repository will later be published. The example address is intentionally a placeholder.


6.12.4 Step 3 — create the initial files
printf '%s\n' \
  '# Mini workflow engineering lab' \
  '' \
  'A local Git exercise using synthetic data only.' \
  > README.md

printf '%s\n' \
  'work/' \
  'results/' \
  '.nextflow/' \
  '.nextflow.log*' \
  '.env' \
  '*.key' \
  '.DS_Store' \
  > .gitignore
Create paths that should be ignored:
mkdir -p work results
printf 'temporary task state\n' > work/task.txt
printf 'generated output\n' > results/result.txt
Inspect:
git status --short
git check-ignore -v work/task.txt results/result.txt
Only .gitignore and README.md should appear as untracked. The other command should identify the ignore rules.


6.12.5 Step 4 — stage and inspect the first snapshot
Stage explicit files:
git add .gitignore README.md
Do not make git add . your only habit. It can be appropriate after inspection, but explicit paths make the intended scope obvious to a beginner.
Review all three views:
git status
git diff
git diff --staged
git diff should be empty because there are no unstaged edits. The staged diff should show the two new files.


6.12.6 Step 5 — create the first commit
git commit -m "chore: initialize the learning repository"
Verify the result:
git status
git log --oneline --decorate
git show --stat HEAD
git ls-files
The working tree should be clean, and exactly .gitignore and README.md should be tracked.


6.12.7 Step 6 — create a focused second change
Add an analytical plan:
printf '%s\n' \
  '# Planned workflow' \
  '' \
  '1. Validate paired synthetic FASTQ inputs.' \
  '2. Run read quality control.' \
  '3. Trim adapters and low-quality ends.' \
  '4. Align reads to a declared reference.' \
  '5. Validate the sorted BAM and summarize mapping.' \
  > workflow.md
Inspect the state:
git status --short
git diff
workflow.md is untracked, so normal git diff will not display its content. Read it directly, then stage it:
cat workflow.md
git add workflow.md
git diff --staged
Commit it:
git commit -m "docs: add the planned analysis stages"


6.12.8 Step 7 — prove the acceptance conditions
git status --short
git log --oneline --decorate -2
git ls-files
git show --stat HEAD
git show --stat HEAD~1
Acceptance criteria:

git status --short produces no output;
the log contains two meaningful commits;
three files are tracked;
the newest commit contains only workflow.md; and
the first commit contains only .gitignore and README.md.

Save interview evidence without inventing it:
{
  printf '%s\n' '=== STATUS ==='
  git status
  printf '%s\n' '=== HISTORY ==='
  git log --oneline --decorate -2
  printf '%s\n' '=== TRACKED FILES ==='
  git ls-files
  printf '%s\n' '=== LATEST COMMIT ==='
  git show --stat --oneline HEAD
} > git-practice-evidence.txt
This evidence file is initially untracked. Decide whether it is a useful small project artifact before adding it; do not automatically create a third commit.

text:
6.13 Read a diff rather than merely looking at colors
A simplified patch looks like this:
diff --git a/workflow.md b/workflow.md
new file mode 100644
--- /dev/null
+++ b/workflow.md
@@ -0,0 +1,3 @@
+# Planned workflow
+
+1. Validate paired synthetic FASTQ inputs.
Interpretation:

a/ and b/ label the compared sides;
/dev/null indicates the file did not exist on the old side;
+ lines are additions;
- lines would be removals; and
the hunk header describes affected line ranges.

Green text is not automatically good and red text is not automatically bad. Review meaning: a one-line deletion can remove a validation check, and a hundred-line addition can be generated noise.

section: 6.14 Commit messages are part of the evidence
text:
6.14 Commit messages are part of the evidence
A useful message completes this sentence:

If applied, this commit will …

Examples:
docs: record synthetic fixture provenance
fix: fail when paired FASTQ input is incomplete
test: add missing-reference negative case
build: pin samtools container digest
Avoid messages such as stuff, changes, final, or AI update. The message should describe the change, not the mood of the author.
A commit should normally represent one coherent reason for change. Small does not mean one line; it means reviewable and conceptually focused.

text:
6.16 Common beginner failures

6.16.1 “I committed, but my new file is missing”
git commit records staged content, not every visible file. Use:
git status
git ls-files
Then stage the intended file and review git diff --staged.


6.16.2 “I added a pattern, but the file is still tracked”
.gitignore mainly affects untracked paths. First determine why the file was tracked and whether removing it from future snapshots is appropriate. Do not copy an index-removal command without understanding its effect.


6.16.3 “My result directory disappeared”
Git does not track empty directories, and ignored/generated directories may not exist in a fresh clone. Scripts should create required output directories.


6.16.4 “I initialized Git in the wrong directory”
Stop before committing. Inspect:
pwd
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
git status
Do not delete an unexpected .git directory until you know whether it contains valuable history and have confirmed the exact path.


6.16.5 “Git rejected my commit identity”
Configure a name and email locally, inspect them and retry. This is independent of GitHub login.

title: 6  Git mental model and first repository
text:
6.17 Reviewing AI-generated Git instructions
AI often proposes commands that produce a desired final state while destroying useful evidence. Be suspicious of unexplained commands containing:
reset --hard
clean -fd
checkout -- <path>
restore --source ...
push --force
filter-repo
These commands have legitimate uses, but they can discard work or rewrite history. They are not beginner troubleshooting defaults.
Before running any Git command suggested by AI, require answers to:

What repository root will it affect?
Does it modify the working tree, staging area, commits or remote history?
Which exact paths or branches are targeted?
Can uncommitted content be lost?
Is the operation recoverable, and from what evidence?
What read-only command shows the current state first?

Prefer diagnosis with status, diff, log, show, branch and rev-parse before mutation.

text:
6.18 Hands-on exercise: audit an AI-authored change
In your practice repository, ask an AI system to propose one paragraph for the README explaining why synthetic data is used. Do not let it commit for you.
Then:

inspect git status --short;
inspect the unstaged patch with git diff;
check the text for claims the project does not demonstrate;
edit or reject unsupported claims;
stage only README.md;
inspect git diff --staged;
write a commit message describing your accepted change; and
prove the final working tree is clean.

Create ai-change-review.md outside the practice repository or leave it untracked. Record:
# AI change review

## Requested change
## Files the AI proposed changing
## Claims independently verified
## Claims corrected or rejected
## Final staged scope
## Commit ID
## Post-commit status
The important skill is not producing the paragraph. It is controlling scope, validating meaning and establishing traceable acceptance.

title: 6  Git mental model and first repository
text:
6.19 Ten interview questions

6.19.1 1. What is the difference between the working tree, staging area and repository?


Model answer

The working tree contains the files currently checked out for editing. The staging area holds the exact content proposed for the next commit. The local repository stores commits, references and history under .git. Saving, staging and committing are therefore three different state transitions.



6.19.2 2. Why can git diff be empty when git status shows a new file?


Model answer

Normal git diff compares tracked working-tree content with the index. An untracked file has no indexed version to compare, so its content is not shown. I inspect the file directly, stage it intentionally and then use git diff --staged.



6.19.3 3. What does git add actually do?


Model answer

It copies the selected content into the index as part of the proposed next snapshot. It does not create a commit, upload anything to GitHub or permanently save all future edits to that file.



6.19.4 4. Is a Git commit a diff or a snapshot?


Model answer

Git’s model is snapshot-based: a commit refers to a complete tree of recorded content plus metadata and parent relationships. Git efficiently stores and displays differences, which is why users often experience commits as patches.



6.19.5 5. What is a branch, and what does HEAD mean?


Model answer

A branch is a movable reference to a commit. HEAD normally identifies the currently checked-out branch, which in turn points to the current commit. A new commit advances that branch reference.



6.19.6 6. Why is .gitignore not a security control?


Model answer

It only influences which untracked paths Git normally reports or stages. It does not encrypt files, prevent another program from reading them, remove already tracked content or erase old commits. Exposed credentials must be revoked or rotated even if an ignore rule is later added.



6.19.7 7. Which bioinformatics artifacts would you track, and which would you exclude?


Model answer

I track reviewable source, configuration, environment/container specifications, tests, documentation, provenance and small permitted fixtures. I exclude sensitive data, secrets, large raw/generated files, workflow caches, local environments and container binaries. Exact choices follow governance, licensing, reproducibility and repository-size requirements.



6.19.8 8. Does a clean working tree prove the analysis is reproducible?


Model answer

No. It only says tracked working-tree and staged content match the selected commit and there are no reported untracked changes. Reproducibility also needs inputs, dependencies, parameters, runtime, references, provenance and validation evidence.



6.19.9 9. How would you verify what a commit contains before sharing it?


Model answer

Before committing I use git status and git diff --staged. After committing I use git show --stat <commit> for scope and git show <commit> for the patch, plus git ls-files when tracked-file inventory matters. I also scan for secrets, sensitive data and unintended generated files.



6.19.10 10. Why should an AI not automatically stage and commit every change it generates?


Model answer

Generation is not review. The AI may change unrelated files, include secrets, invent claims, misunderstand repository policy or bundle several concerns. A human or authorized review process should inspect the patch, test behavior, control staged scope and choose a message that accurately records the accepted change.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.1 Why a biologist should care
A manual analysis often becomes a notebook of commands: run QC, trim reads, align, sort, deduplicate and calculate summaries. The commands may be correct, but the notebook does not automatically remember which outputs belong to which inputs, which steps may run together, or which completed work can be reused.
Nextflow describes those relationships. It launches ordinary programs when their declared inputs become available, records task evidence and connects outputs to downstream steps.
Nextflow does not perform alignment, trimming or methylation calling. Those jobs belong to tools such as Bismark, Bowtie2, Trim Galore and FastQC.

21  Nextflow mental model

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.2 Engineering objective
Learn this sentence:

Nextflow is a workflow engine that moves values and files through declared process contracts and delegates each resulting task to an executor.

That sentence contains the important layers:
pipeline code     process contracts and data connections
software          FastQC, Bismark, SAMtools, ordinary shell commands
runtime           Conda, Docker, Singularity/Apptainer
executor          local computer, Slurm, cloud batch service
storage           inputs, work directories, published results, caches
Changing the executor should not change the scientific intention of the workflow. It changes where tasks run.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.3 Start from a manual command
Suppose you can count lines in one file manually:
wc -l sample.txt > sample.line_count.txt
A workflow representation must answer:

What file is the input?
What command runs?
What output proves completion?
What should receive that output next?
Where should the task run and with which software and resources?

Nextflow separates these answers instead of hiding them in one long script.

21  Nextflow mental model

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.4 Process versus task
A process is a reusable recipe. A task is one execution of that recipe for one set of inputs.
process COUNT_LINES
        │
        ├── task for alpha.txt
        ├── task for beta.txt
        └── task for gamma.txt
This distinction explains Slurm output that surprises beginners. One biological sample can generate multiple scheduler jobs because FastQC, trimming, alignment and reporting are different tasks. Conversely, one process can generate 30 tasks when 30 samples arrive.
crumbs: Part VI — Nextflow DSL2 from first process to complete pipeline
21  Nextflow mental model

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.5 Processes are contracts
A process normally has four important sections:
process COUNT_LINES {
    input:
    path sample_file

    output:
    path 'count.txt'

    script:
    """
    wc -l < ${sample_file} > count.txt
    """
}

input declares what the task needs.
output declares what successful execution must create.
script contains the command executed by the task.
directives placed above input, such as cpus, memory, container, tag and publishDir, describe execution behavior.

If the command exits zero but does not create count.txt, the process fails because its output contract was not satisfied.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.6 Values, paths and tuples
A channel item has a shape. Say the shape aloud before writing compact syntax.



Shape
Example
Typical use




value
"mouse_A"
sample ID, threshold, mode


path
/data/mouse_A_R1.fastq.gz
a staged file


tuple
["mouse_A", R1, R2]
metadata kept with paired files


stream of tuples
one tuple per sample
a cohort



val inputs are ordinary values. path inputs tell Nextflow that a filesystem object must be staged into the task directory. A tuple keeps related values together while they travel through the workflow.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.7 Channels carry data
A channel is not a directory and not a CSV file. It is the runtime connection through which values move.
paired FASTQ channel
        │
        ├──► raw QC
        │
        └──► trimming ──► alignment ──► BAM QC
When two independent processes receive the same input channel, Nextflow may run them concurrently. When alignment needs trimmed reads, it waits for trimming. You describe dependencies through data, not by manually waiting for job IDs.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.8 Workflow block
DSL2 connects channels and processes inside workflow:
workflow {
    samples = channel.fromPath('data/*.txt')
    COUNT_LINES(samples)
}
This reads as: create a stream of paths, then invoke COUNT_LINES for each item. The process definition says how; the workflow block says how things connect.

21  Nextflow mental model

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.9 Task work directories
Every task runs in an isolated hashed directory below work/:
work/a3/7be2fa...
├── .command.sh
├── .command.run
├── .command.log
├── .command.out
├── .command.err
├── .exitcode
├── staged inputs
└── declared outputs
Isolation prevents 30 samples from overwriting one another’s output.txt. The hash also contributes to caching. The short string printed beside a process, such as [a3/7be2fa], points to this directory; it is not a scheduler job ID.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.11 Executor mental model
With the local executor, Nextflow starts task processes on the current machine. With the Slurm executor, Nextflow submits task wrappers to Slurm. The small Nextflow controller must remain alive to observe completed tasks and submit downstream work.
Nextflow controller
    ├── submits FASTQC task ─────► Slurm
    ├── submits TRIM task ───────► Slurm
    ├── observes their outputs
    └── submits ALIGN task ──────► Slurm
The controller is not the alignment job. Requesting 4 GB for the controller does not force Bismark to use 4 GB; process directives control task resources.
crumbs: Part VI — Nextflow DSL2 from first process to complete pipeline
21  Nextflow mental model

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.12 Cache and -resume
For each task, Nextflow computes a cache key from relevant inputs, process code, configuration and environment information. A matching successful task can be reused with -resume while its work directory and cache metadata remain.
Resume is selective recomputation, not magic checkpointing inside a running aligner. A failed alignment normally restarts that task; already completed upstream tasks may be cached.

title: 21  Nextflow mental model
text:
21.13 Verification checkpoint
For this graph:
reads ──► FASTQC_RAW
  └─────► TRIM ──► FASTQC_TRIMMED
                └► ALIGN ──► BAM_QC
Predict before reading the answer:

FASTQC_RAW and TRIM may begin together.
FASTQC_TRIMMED waits for TRIM.
ALIGN waits for TRIM.
FASTQC_TRIMMED and ALIGN may run together after trimmed reads exist.
BAM_QC waits for ALIGN.

If you can explain those statements using data availability rather than line order, the core mental model is working.

title: 22  Your first Nextflow process
section: 22.4 Build it: read the complete file
text:
22.4 Build it: read the complete file
Open 01-hello.nf:
nextflow.enable.dsl=2

params.name = 'biologist'

process MAKE_GREETING {
    tag "${name}"
    publishDir 'results/01-hello', mode: 'copy'

    input:
    val name

    output:
    path 'greeting.txt'

    script:
    """
    echo "Hello, ${name}!" > greeting.txt
    """
}

workflow {
    MAKE_GREETING(params.name)
}

22.4.1 Read the syntax

nextflow.enable.dsl=2 makes the DSL generation explicit for learners.
params.name declares a command-line parameter with a default.
MAKE_GREETING is the process definition.
tag places a meaningful value in logs instead of only a task hash.
val name accepts an ordinary value.
path 'greeting.txt' declares the file that success must produce.
the triple-quoted block is the shell script.
MAKE_GREETING(params.name) invokes the process in the workflow.
publishDir ... mode: 'copy' copies the selected result out of work/.

This book uses process-level publishDir because it remains common in production and nf-core pipelines and is supported by the validated tutorial version. Newer Nextflow training also teaches workflow-level output publishing; learn to recognize both and follow the version policy of the project you join.

22.5 Run it
nextflow run 01-hello.nf --name Ada

Expected status shape:
[ab/cdef12] MAKE_GREETING (Ada) | 1 of 1 ✔
The hash will differ. Verify the published result:
cat results/01-hello/greeting.txt
Expected:
Hello, Ada!

title: 22  Your first Nextflow process
text:
22.6 Inspect task anatomy
Ask Nextflow for the most recent task directory:
nextflow log last -f hash,name,status,workdir
Copy the printed work-directory path into a variable:
TASK_DIR=/absolute/path/printed/by/nextflow
ls -la "$TASK_DIR"
Inspect evidence one file at a time:
cat "$TASK_DIR/.command.sh"
cat "$TASK_DIR/.command.log"
cat "$TASK_DIR/.exitcode"

.command.sh is the scientific command generated for the process.
.command.run is Nextflow’s execution wrapper, including staging/runtime.
.command.out and .command.err capture standard streams.
.command.log combines task output useful for diagnosis.
.exitcode should contain 0 for success.

Do not edit files in a task directory to “fix” a run. Fix tracked pipeline code or configuration, then rerun.

nextflow run 01-hello.nf --name Ada -resume

nextflow run 01-hello.nf --name Grace -resume

title: 23  Channels, tuples and paired files
text:
23.4 One path input
Run the second example:
nextflow run 02-one-file.nf
cat results/02-one-file/sequence.character_count.txt
The important lines are:
params.input = "${projectDir}/data/sequence.txt"

workflow {
    input_file = file(params.input, checkIfExists: true)
    COUNT_CHARACTERS(input_file)
}
projectDir is the pipeline-code directory, making the default independent of the terminal’s launch directory. file(..., checkIfExists: true) converts the parameter into a path value and fails early if it is absent.
The process declares path sequence. Nextflow stages that file into an isolated task directory. The script should refer to ${sequence}, not reach back to an undeclared absolute path.

23.5 Many files create many tasks
Run:
nextflow run 03-many-samples.nf
find results/03-many-samples -type f -maxdepth 1 -print -exec cat {} \;
The channel is built in two steps:
samples = channel
    .fromPath(params.input, checkIfExists: true)
    .map { sample_file -> tuple(sample_file.baseName, sample_file) }
Read the shape transition:
before map: path
after map:  [sample_id, path]
For alpha.txt, the tuple is conceptually:
["alpha", /.../data/samples/alpha.txt]
The process contract must match that shape:
input:
tuple val(sample_id), path(sample_file)
Nextflow creates one COUNT_LINES task per tuple. The sample_id travels with the staged file and is used in output naming.

23.9 Operators are shape transformations
Do not memorize operators as punctuation. Write their input and output shapes.








Operator
Question it answers
Example shape change




map
How should each item change?

filter
Which items continue?

collect
When do I need all items together?

                       ┌────────────► FASTQC_RAW
paired FASTQ tuples ───┤
                       └────────────► TRIM_GALORE
                                          │
                            ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                            ▼                           ▼
                     FASTQC_TRIMMED                 ALIGN_SORT
                                                        │
                                                        ▼
                                                      BAM_QC
Translate the trusted manual baseline one process at a time. Do not write all five processes and debug them simultaneously.

24.5.1 Process 1: raw QC
Contract:
input:  sample ID plus R1/R2 paths
action: FastQC on both mates
output: two HTML reports and two ZIP archives, still labeled by sample
The process should not search the filesystem itself. The workflow gives it the two declared files.


24.5.2 Process 2: paired trimming
Contract:
input:  sample ID plus paired raw FASTQs
action: Trim Galore in paired mode
output: sample ID plus paired trimmed FASTQs and trimming reports
The paired relationship must survive. Do not emit R1 and R2 into unrelated channels and later hope that arrival order reconstructs the pairs.


24.5.3 Branch after trimming
Post-trim FastQC and alignment both consume trimmed reads. They are independent after those files exist, so Nextflow may run them concurrently.


24.5.4 Process 3: post-trim QC
Use the same FastQC operation with a different process name and output location. Raw and trimmed QC answer different questions and must not overwrite one another.


24.5.5 Process 4: align and sort
The trusted manual command may pipe aligner output into samtools sort. Keeping that pipe inside one process avoids writing a large SAM intermediate. The shell must use pipefail; otherwise an aligner failure can be hidden if sorting exits zero on incomplete input.
Contract:
input:  sample ID, trimmed pair and matching reference/index
action: align paired reads and coordinate-sort the alignment
output: sample ID plus sorted BAM and alignment log


24.5.6 Process 5: BAM QC
Index and validate the BAM, then create flagstat and idxstats summaries. Declare the BAM and BAI together when downstream tools require both.

26.4 Fail before analysis with input validation
Supply a pattern that matches nothing:
nextflow run 04-paired-reads.nf \
  --reads 'data/reads/DOES_NOT_EXIST_{R1,R2}.fastq'
Expected outcome: nonzero exit and an error indicating that no files matched. That is a good failure because checkIfExists: true stops before task execution.

nextflow run 04-paired-reads.nf \
  --reads 'data/reads/DOES_NOT_EXIST_{R1,R2}.fastq'

26.5 Diagnose in evidence order
When a real task fails, inspect:

the concise terminal error;
.nextflow.log for controller context;
the indicated task directory;
.command.sh for the generated scientific command;
.command.err and .command.log for tool/runtime messages;
.command.run for container, staging and scheduler details;
.exitcode when created;
scheduler state/accounting for termination, memory and time evidence.

Separate the failure layer:



Evidence
Likely layer




Java crash before launch
host/Nextflow runtime


image pull or bind error
container runtime/storage


pending with scheduler reason
executor/site policy


exit 137 or OOM event
task memory/resource policy


tool rejects FASTQ
input/tool/scientific layer


missing declared output
process contract or tool behavior

  -profile local \

27.6 Controller script
A sanitized controller has this shape:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=nextflow-controller
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x.%j.err

set -euo pipefail

source /etc/profile.d/lmod.sh
module purge
module load java/xxx
module load singularity/xxx

export NXF_HOME=/project/xxx/nextflow_home
export NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR=/project/xxx/singularity_cache

nextflow run . \
  -profile slurm_singularity \
  -c conf/site.local.config \
  -resume \
  -with-trace "logs/${SLURM_JOB_ID}.trace.tsv"
Submit from a predictable directory:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch bin/run_pipeline.sbatch
The printed ID belongs to the controller. Nextflow task jobs receive their own Slurm IDs.

text:
27.10 Real-world WGBS case study
A sanitized production qualification followed three gates:

tiny nf-core smoke test for installation and container/scheduler plumbing;
10-million-read-pair real WGBS pilot for reference compatibility and performance measurement;
one complete paired sample for whole-sample QC, runtime, storage and MultiQC acceptance before a 30-sample cohort.

The pilot showed that alignment dominated runtime and efficiently used 12 CPUs, with peak memory well below its 72 GB request. A shared-resource policy limited future concurrent Bismark alignments to ten. That limit controls cohort impact; it does not split or independently deduplicate a biological sample.
The complete-sample qualification was launched in a separate project root with its own work/, caches, logs and results. The result must not be presented as validated until the final success marker, BAM/BAI, methylation coverage, MultiQC, trace, checksums and private provenance have been reviewed.
This case teaches a general rule: benchmark small, qualify one complete unit, then scale under a measured concurrency policy.

It finished, failed or was cancelled. Inspect the final controller log and accounting. Empty squeue is not proof of success.


27.11.2 Task remains pending
Read NODELIST(REASON) or scontrol show job. A request for excessive memory, invalid account or dependency differs from ordinary queue wait.

Relaunch the same workflow with identical parameters, work directory and -resume after diagnosing the stop. Completed matching tasks should be cached. For future cohorts, choose a longer permitted controller limit or sequential waves with adequate margin.


27.11.4 Home quota breaks Nextflow or image pulls
Move NXF_HOME, work and container caches to approved project/scratch storage. Remove corrupt partial downloads only after resolving exact targets.

34.6 Phase 1: establish a usable host environment

34.6.1 Inventory before installation
On a compute node, inspect rather than assume:
command -v java
command -v nextflow
command -v singularity
command -v apptainer
module spider java
module spider singularity
The observed cluster supplied Java and Singularity modules but no Nextflow module. The user’s existing Conda Java crashed during JVM initialization. This was a host-runtime failure before any workflow or WGBS code ran.


34.6.2 Lesson: use a validated Java module
source /etc/profile.d/lmod.sh
module purge
module load java/xxx
module load singularity/xxx

java -version
singularity --version
Module names are site-specific. The public repository must use placeholders; the real names belong in an ignored environment file.


34.6.3 Failure: Nextflow framework download exceeded home quota
The first launcher attempt wrote its framework JAR below a small home directory and failed with Disk quota exceeded, leaving an invalid/corrupt JAR.
The correction was to put the runtime home on project storage:
export PROJECT=/project/xxx/wgbs-project
export NXF_HOME="$PROJECT/nextflow_home"
export NXF_VER=25.10.7
export NXF_TEMP="$PROJECT/tmp"

mkdir -p "$NXF_HOME" "$NXF_TEMP"
NXF_HOME stores Nextflow framework and asset data. It is not the same as the pipeline’s work/ directory.


34.6.4 Failure: launcher location and framework version were confused
The small nextflow launcher script and the downloaded framework JAR are different files. Running ./nextflow works only from the directory containing the executable launcher, or through its absolute path:
/project/xxx/wgbs-project/bin/nextflow -version
Verify the version under the same NXF_HOME and NXF_VER that production will use.


34.6.5 Failure: incompatible Nextflow/plugin versions
An early pinned Nextflow release was too old for the nf-schema plugin required by methylseq. Jumping to a newer unvalidated framework exposed a separate legacy configuration-parsing incompatibility. The working response was not “always use latest”; it was to identify and pin a compatible combination, then test it.
The qualification recorded:
Nextflow:          25.10.7
nf-core/methylseq: 4.2.0
Singularity CE:    4.0.3
Bismark:           0.25.1 (containerized task)
These are case-study facts, not permanent universal requirements.

34.8 Phase 3: run the tiny nf-core smoke test
The smoke test used versioned pipeline and container profiles:
nextflow run nf-core/methylseq \
  -r 4.2.0 \
  -profile test,singularity \
  -c conf/slurm.config \
  --outdir results/nfcore-test \
  -work-dir work \
  -with-trace logs/smoke.trace.tsv \
  -with-report logs/smoke.report.html \
  -with-timeline logs/smoke.timeline.html
The test profile downloaded a tiny test genome and built the matching Bismark index inside a task work directory. This explains how alignment succeeded even though the project’s human reference did not yet contain Bisulfite_Genome.
Smoke-test acceptance required:
find results/nfcore-test -type f -name '*.cov.gz' -print
find results/nfcore-test -type f -name '*.bam' -print
find results/nfcore-test -type f -name 'multiqc_report.html' -print
The test proved workflow plumbing and expected output types. It did not prove that the human GRCh38 reference was ready.

section: 34.9 Phase 4: prepare the correct Bismark reference
text:
34.9 Phase 4: prepare the correct Bismark reference
The existing GRCh38 directory contained BWA and BWA-Meth indexes. Those cannot substitute for a Bismark/Bowtie2 bisulfite index.
A valid Bismark reference directory has this shape:
bismark_species_assembly/
├── reference.fa
└── Bisulfite_Genome/
    ├── CT_conversion/
    │   ├── BS_CT.1.bt2
    │   ├── ...
    │   └── BS_CT.rev.2.bt2
    └── GA_conversion/
        ├── BS_GA.1.bt2
        ├── ...
        └── BS_GA.rev.2.bt2
The FASTA was copied—not symlinked—into the self-contained index directory so the same path remained visible inside container bind mounts. Its checksum was verified before and after copying:
sha256sum reference.fa
The index was built through a Slurm task using the same containerized Bismark version as the workflow. Acceptance required all 12 Bowtie2 index files and the matching FASTA. A partial Bisulfite_Genome from a failed attempt was preserved with a .failed.JOB_ID suffix for diagnosis rather than presented as valid.
For another species, repeat the procedure with that species and assembly. Never reuse a human index for mouse, or an index from another assembly release.

34.10 Phase 5: create a synchronized 10M-pair pilot
The pilot sampled the same first 10,000,000 records from R1 and R2:
seqkit head --number 10000000 SAMPLE_R1.fastq.gz \
  --out-file SAMPLE_10M_R1.fastq.gz

seqkit head --number 10000000 SAMPLE_R2.fastq.gz \
  --out-file SAMPLE_10M_R2.fastq.gz
Verification:
seqkit stats SAMPLE_10M_R1.fastq.gz SAMPLE_10M_R2.fastq.gz
gzip -t SAMPLE_10M_R1.fastq.gz SAMPLE_10M_R2.fastq.gz
Both mates contained exactly 10,000,000 reads of length 151. Taking the same record count from ordered mates preserves pairing without loading complete FASTQs into memory.

34.10.1 Pilot samplesheet
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,genome
SAMPLE_10M,/project/xxx/subsets/SAMPLE_10M_R1.fastq.gz,/project/xxx/subsets/SAMPLE_10M_R2.fastq.gz,


34.10.2 Pilot parameters
input: /project/xxx/samplesheets/SAMPLE_10M.csv
outdir: /project/xxx/results/SAMPLE_10M

aligner: bismark
fasta: /project/xxx/reference/bismark_grch38/reference.fa
bismark_index: /project/xxx/reference/bismark_grch38
Resource policy belongs in Nextflow configuration, not invented YAML keys. The pipeline’s Bismark alignment defaults requested 12 CPUs and 72 GB, with an eight-day task ceiling.

34.12 Projection to a complete sample
The representative full pair contained 100.83 GB compressed versus 1.327 GB for the pilot, a ratio of about 75.97.
Simple linear projection:
complete alignment ≈ pilot alignment × 75.97 ≈ 5.6 days
complete workflow  ≈ pilot workflow  × 75.97 ≈ 6.5 days
Planning range: approximately 6–8 days, excluding queue delay and retries. This is a model, not a promise; compression, trimming, duplication, filesystem contention and sample complexity may scale nonlinearly.

34.13 Phase 6: create reusable production controls

34.13.1 Private site environment
PROJECT=/storage/xxx/wgbs-production
JAVA_MODULE=java/xxx
CONTAINER_MODULE=singularity/xxx
CONTAINER_PROFILE=singularity
NEXTFLOW_VERSION=25.10.7
METHYLSEQ_VERSION=4.2.0
NEXTFLOW_BIN=/absolute/path/to/bin/nextflow
This real file is ignored by Git. A tracked .example file contains only placeholders.


34.13.2 Shared-cluster concurrency policy
process {
    withName: BISMARK_ALIGN {
        maxForks = 10
    }
}

executor {
    queueSize = 30
    submitRateLimit = '2 sec'
}
Interpretation:

at most ten Bismark alignment tasks run concurrently;
up to 30 tasks may be managed in the executor queue; and
submissions are rate-limited as scheduler courtesy.

With 12 CPUs and 72 GB requested per alignment, ten concurrent alignments imply up to 120 CPUs and 720 GB requested memory. The policy was chosen to avoid occupying an entire shared cluster.

section: 34.18 Use the companion repository for your own WGBS analysis
text:
34.18 Use the companion repository for your own WGBS analysis
The public WGBS methylseq pipeline repository is the reusable implementation behind this case study. A new user can clone or fork it, but cannot safely launch a large cohort without supplying and validating their own infrastructure, reference, inputs and capacity policy.

34.18.1 Clone versus fork
Clone when you want to use the documented workflow without maintaining a public variant:
git clone https://github.com/cjgunase/wgbs-methylseq-pipeline.git
cd wgbs-methylseq-pipeline
git rev-parse HEAD
Fork first when your group intends to maintain reviewed changes, site profiles or additional features. Keep private paths and regulated metadata out of both the original repository and the fork.
Record the commit from git rev-parse HEAD in every run manifest. A Git branch name such as main can move; a commit identifies the code reviewed at launch.


34.18.2 What the repository supplies







Repository component
Purpose




bin/check_environment.sh
Check host prerequisites and report actionable failures


bin/run_nfcore_test.sbatch
Run the tiny bundled methylseq test through Slurm/Singularity


bin/build_bismark_index.sbatch
Build a containerized Bismark index from a supplied FASTA


bin/make_samplesheet.sh
Generate paired samplesheet rows from regular R1/R2 filenames


bin/run_pilot.sbatch
Run a real-data subset with the production-like pipeline


bin/preflight.sh
Check paths, pairing, reference/index, output collision and storage


bin/run_production.sbatch
Guarded full-sample/cohort Nextflow controller


bin/monitor_run.sh
Read-only Slurm/controller progress summary


conf/*.example
Portable templates without private site values


params/*.example.yaml
Analysis parameter templates


assets/run-manifest.template.md
Private execution/provenance record


docs/
Beginner explanations, troubleshooting and acceptance gates



The repository does not supply your sequencing data, reference assembly, scheduler account, storage allocation, Java installation or permission to use the cluster.


34.18.3 Host prerequisites
For a Slurm HPC system, obtain or verify:

Java compatible with the selected Nextflow version;
a pinned Nextflow launcher/framework;
Git and a download tool such as curl;
Slurm commands including sbatch and squeue;
Singularity or Apptainer allowed by the site;
shared storage readable from compute nodes; and
sufficient quota for inputs, work/, results, framework and image caches.

Bioinformatics tools such as FastQC, Trim Galore, Bismark and SAMtools are provided by nf-core’s versioned containers. Users normally do not rebuild one large custom container for this workflow. The first run downloads the required images; offline sites must pre-stage them according to local policy.
On a laptop or workstation, follow the repository’s local installation guide and use Docker where supported. Production-scale WGBS generally requires an HPC or cloud environment with adequate storage and scheduler capacity.


34.18.4 Step 1: create the private site environment
From the repository root:
cp conf/site.env.example conf/site.env
Edit the ignored conf/site.env:
PROJECT=/project/xxx/wgbs-pilot
JAVA_MODULE=java/xxx
CONTAINER_MODULE=singularity/xxx
CONTAINER_PROFILE=singularity
NEXTFLOW_VERSION=25.10.7
METHYLSEQ_VERSION=4.2.0
NEXTFLOW_BIN=/absolute/path/to/bin/nextflow
Values shown are placeholders except the versions validated in this case study. If your site requires different versions, treat that as a new compatibility combination: rerun the environment check and smoke test and record the result.
Place PROJECT, NXF_HOME, work data and container caches on an appropriate large filesystem—not automatically in a quota-limited home directory.


34.18.5 Step 2: verify the host on a compute node
Request a small interactive allocation using your site’s documented syntax, then run:
bash bin/check_environment.sh
Proceed only when Java, Nextflow, the container runtime and Slurm tools report OK. A missing bioinformatics executable on the host is not necessarily an error because task software runs in containers.


34.18.6 Step 3: run the tiny infrastructure smoke test
mkdir -p logs
sbatch bin/run_nfcore_test.sbatch
Record the controller job ID, monitor it and require the final success marker. Confirm that the test produces BAM/BAI, .cov.gz, FastQC, Bismark reports and MultiQC. This stage uses nf-core test data and its test reference; it does not validate your species assembly or sequencing data.


34.18.7 Step 4: prepare a species- and assembly-specific reference
Choose a traceable FASTA. Record:

species and assembly name/release;
authoritative source and retrieval date;
primary/alternate/decoy content decisions;
chromosome naming convention; and
SHA-256 checksum.

Build a self-contained index:
sbatch bin/build_bismark_index.sbatch \
  /absolute/path/to/reference.fa \
  /absolute/path/to/bismark_species_assembly
The destination should contain the FASTA plus Bisulfite_Genome/CT_conversion and GA_conversion, each with six Bowtie2 index files. The index must match the exact FASTA supplied to methylseq.
For mouse, plant or another organism, substitute the correct assembly and build a new index. The workflow is species-independent; the reference is not.


34.18.8 Step 5: prepare and validate input metadata
Expected paired filename pattern for the generator:
SAMPLE_001_R1.fastq.gz
SAMPLE_001_R2.fastq.gz
Generate a samplesheet:
bash bin/make_samplesheet.sh \
  /absolute/path/to/fastq-directory \
  /absolute/path/to/study.samplesheet.csv
Inspect it rather than trusting generation:
head /absolute/path/to/study.samplesheet.csv
wc -l /absolute/path/to/study.samplesheet.csv
The methylseq 4.2.0 paired-end shape used here is:
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,genome
SAMPLE_001,/data/SAMPLE_001_R1.fastq.gz,/data/SAMPLE_001_R2.fastq.gz,
If filenames do not follow the supported pattern, create and validate the CSV deliberately. Confirm every sample ID, R1/R2 association, file existence, readability and study-metadata mapping. The generator cannot detect a FASTQ that was mislabeled before it reached the directory.


34.18.9 Step 6: run a synchronized real-data pilot
Create the same number of records from R1 and R2 on a compute node. The repository guide uses 10,000,000 read pairs:
seqkit head --number 10000000 SAMPLE_001_R1.fastq.gz \
  --out-file SAMPLE_001_10M_R1.fastq.gz

seqkit head --number 10000000 SAMPLE_001_R2.fastq.gz \
  --out-file SAMPLE_001_10M_R2.fastq.gz

seqkit stats SAMPLE_001_10M_R1.fastq.gz SAMPLE_001_10M_R2.fastq.gz
gzip -t SAMPLE_001_10M_R1.fastq.gz SAMPLE_001_10M_R2.fastq.gz
Copy and edit the pilot parameter template:
cp params/pilot.example.yaml /private/path/pilot.params.yaml
Set input, a new outdir, aligner: bismark, the FASTA and its matching bismark_index. Submit:
sbatch bin/run_pilot.sbatch /private/path/pilot.params.yaml
Review trace, required outputs and MultiQC. Use the pilot for engineering throughput and compatibility—not final duplication, coverage or biology.


34.18.10 Step 7: configure one complete-sample qualification
Do not use the cohort samplesheet yet. Select one representative complete paired sample and create a new production project root with separate work, results, logs and caches.
Create private production files:
cp conf/production.env.example conf/production.env
cp conf/production.shared.config.example conf/production.local.config
cp params/production.example.yaml params/one-sample.production.yaml
Edit every placeholder. The parameter file should resemble:
input: /storage/xxx/samplesheets/one-sample.csv
outdir: /storage/xxx/results/SAMPLE_001

aligner: bismark
fasta: /storage/xxx/reference/bismark_species_assembly/reference.fa
bismark_index: /storage/xxx/reference/bismark_species_assembly
Preflight using the production environment explicitly:
SITE_ENV=conf/production.env \
  bash bin/preflight.sh params/one-sample.production.yaml
Resolve every STOP and review every warning. Submit from the repository root:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch bin/run_production.sbatch params/one-sample.production.yaml
Do not call the repository qualified for your environment merely because the job started. Apply the complete-sample acceptance gate in this chapter.


34.18.11 Step 8: preserve the exact launch record
At submission, create a private run manifest and snapshot the submitted files:
mkdir -p /storage/xxx/run_manifests
cp assets/run-manifest.template.md \
  /storage/xxx/run_manifests/JOB_ID.run-manifest.md
cp /private/path/samplesheet.csv \
  /storage/xxx/run_manifests/JOB_ID.samplesheet.csv
cp /private/path/params.yaml \
  /storage/xxx/run_manifests/JOB_ID.params.yaml
sha256sum /storage/xxx/run_manifests/JOB_ID.samplesheet.csv
sha256sum /storage/xxx/run_manifests/JOB_ID.params.yaml
git rev-parse HEAD
Complete the manifest with the reference checksum, workflow revisions, container/software evidence, deviations, task trace and QC disposition.


34.18.12 Step 9: prepare the cohort only after qualification
When the representative full sample passes:

replace pilot projections with measured full-sample runtime, peak RSS, CPU efficiency, I/O and storage;
inspect sample-size variability across the cohort;
review conf/production.local.config with the HPC team;
choose concurrency that respects shared resources and controller wall-time;
create a new unused cohort output directory;
rerun preflight with the complete samplesheet; and
submit the same pinned workflow/reference configuration.

The example policy limits Bismark alignment to ten concurrent samples. It is a starting point derived from one cluster and pilot—not a universal safe value. Sites with different node sizes, fair-share rules or memory must choose their own reviewed limit.


34.18.13 Step 10: monitor, resume and clean deliberately
Monitor the controller and task jobs:
bash bin/monitor_run.sh CONTROLLER_JOB_ID
If the controller or a task fails, diagnose before changing configuration. Relaunch the same run with the same work directory and -resume through the guarded launcher. Do not delete work/ while recovery or review remains possible.
Clean work data only after:

every required result and report is verified;
provenance and checksums are complete;
outputs have the required backup/retention protection;
no resume is expected; and
the exact cleanup target has been reviewed.



34.18.14 What users should customize—and what they should not







Customize for your project/site
Keep stable unless deliberately revalidated

biological process ordering


Java/container module names
whole-sample deduplication semantics

pairing and samplesheet contracts

reference/index identity requirement

provenance and checksum requirements


reviewed CPU/memory/time/concurrency
smoke → pilot → full-sample gates


optional methylseq parameters justified by assay
pinned versions used for an accepted run



Do not edit cached nf-core pipeline source to make site-specific changes. Use parameters and layered configuration so the upstream revision remains identifiable and updateable.


34.18.15 Honest readiness statement
Before the complete-sample qualification finishes, the correct description is:

The companion repository provides a containerized, Slurm-ready and documented framework. Host bootstrap, the nf-core smoke test, the matching GRCh38 Bismark index and the 10M-pair real-data pilot have been demonstrated. Complete-sample production qualification is in progress.

After a user’s own complete representative sample passes all gates, they may state that the configuration was qualified in that specific environment for that reference, assay, workflow revision and acceptance procedure. They should not generalize that claim automatically to another cluster, species, pipeline version or regulated intended use.

35.5 Build it

35.5.1 1. Create the repository
mkdir -p ~/projects/bioinformatics_projects/ancestryflow
cd ~/projects/bioinformatics_projects/ancestryflow
git init
In your editor, create .gitignore in this directory and save:
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.egg-info/
build/
dist/
.pytest_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/
data/
reference/
results/
work/
.nextflow/
